summary:
West Bengal stands under India's national framework. Parliament's Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill of March 2026 replaced the 2019 law's self-identification route with legal recognition limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals, so trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. Rights activists, among them Akkai Padmashali, describe the amendment as criminalising and an attack on the right to exist, while the government presents it as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018 and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, read to cover gender identity, but same-sex marriage and civil partnership are not available.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024: replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed gender-identity-specific sexual-violence offences that had protected trans persons, and trans people fear a rise in assaults as a result. Identity documents and checkpoints are a live source of friction. In February 2026 the Allahabad High Court granted relief to a trans person asked to take a medical exam by passport authorities; in November 2024 openly transgender law student Sakshi Jain was stopped at Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 by Central Industrial Security Force personnel despite presenting her PAN card. In West Bengal itself, a group of trans women heading to RG Kar Medical College filed an FIR on 18 August 2024 alleging an RPF constable at Rabindra Sadan metro station groped one of them to check her gender and made inappropriate remarks; Metro Railway and the RPF denied the allegations and counter-filed an FIR against the group, while footage showed the trans woman in tears. Transgender persons arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam have recounted degrading treatment in custody.

Assessments of police conduct diverge. The United Kingdom's December 2025 country policy note records limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic; victim interviews documented in June 2024 record abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police issued sweeping guidelines on protecting LGBTQIA+ persons, police sensitisation and a ban on conversion therapy, with directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities; bans from that judgment and from the National Medical Commission in 2022 coexist with clandestine networks still operating.

West Bengal registered 3 of the 7 Transgender Persons Act cases filed nationally in 2021, the highest count that year alongside Assam and Kerala, though national totals remain very small at 20 cases from 2019 to 2023, a figure the report attributes to police-registration bias rather than low incidence. A 2025 survey recorded prevalence of 27.2% physical violence and 22.3% sexual violence against trans people. South Dinajpur police arrested Bangladeshi transgender person Ali Mondal, also known as Bijli Mondal, from Sirajganj district, along with the e-rickshaw driver who brought her across the border, for allegedly infiltrating India, illustrating exposure to immigration enforcement for trans border-crossers.

Facilities and care access are largely set at state level. Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha run transgender welfare boards coordinating housing subsidies, free sex reassignment surgery in public hospitals and pensions, and several states provide targeted welfare, housing and healthcare benefits for hijras. Nationally, the Ayushman Bharat scheme was expanded in April 2024 to cover transition-related healthcare for all members of the transgender community, and in August 2024 the Ministry of Finance clarified that LGBTQ people face no restrictions on opening joint bank accounts or naming partners as beneficiaries. West Bengal is one of the 12 states and union territories that notified a transgender welfare board, but its constituted board operates without a functioning policy framework; nationally, most boards have held fewer than one meeting per year since creation, and the 17 existing boards are mostly running rudderless without a policy framework, compliance mechanism or any power, with several functioning as non-transparent bodies that diffuse demands instead of serving trans people.

Intersex minors remain at risk: reports document a history of infanticide and a strong parental preference for assigning intersex infants male through non-consensual operations, and the Madras High Court ordered Tamil Nadu in April 2019 to ban sex-selective surgeries on intersex infants.

outOfScopeNotes:
Whether West Bengal's transgender welfare board has adopted any operational scheme since the RTI investigation published on 5 November 2024 is not sourced here; the inventory establishes only that the board lacks a functioning policy framework.

The outcome of the counter-FIR filed by Metro Railway and the RPF against the trans women who alleged groping at Rabindra Sadan metro station on 18 August 2024 is unresolved in the inventory.

Whether the March 2026 amendment's recognition limits have been litigated in West Bengal specifically is not sourced; the inventory records only the national text and activist criticism.

The 2025 survey reporting 27.2% physical and 22.3% sexual violence prevalence is cited without a stated sample, geography or methodology in the inventory, so its applicability to West Bengal alone is unresolved.
